The story is told from the perspective of a narrator who harbors unappealing, petty traits: he is consumed by a decades-long, bitter envy of his seemingly perfect college roommate, Q, to the point of keeping a notebook list of Q's nonexistent flaws and secretly eavesdropping on him ten years later, hoping to witness his failure. Despite the narrator's resentment and moral ambiguity, the writer depicts his mindset with great psychological accuracy and humanity. His feelings of inadequacy—feeling like a "rough draft" or merely "solid"—make his obsession completely believable. Furthermore, through the narrator's observations, the story convincingly captures the contrasting perspectives of both Dana (her vulnerable, rising hope) and Q (whose desire to be gentle and conflict-averse leads to a cowardly, catastrophic miscommunication). When the narrator finally witnesses Q's flaw, his shift from schadenfreude to "terrible tenderness" makes him a rich, three-dimensional character.
